title: Metformin in women with type 2 diabetes in pregnancy (MiTy): a multicentre, international, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
authors: Feig DS, Donovan LE, Zinman B, Sanchez JJ, Asztalos E, Ryan EA, et al.
followUp: from randomisation between 6 and 22 weeks' gestation to delivery
population: Pregnant women with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin, at 25 centres in Canada and Australia; 253 assigned metformin and 249 placebo, with complete primary outcome data for 233 (92%) and 240 (96%)
funder: Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute, University of Toronto. The ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT01353391 names Mount Sinai Hospital, Canada as lead sponsor, with University Health Network Toronto, Sunnybrook Research Institute and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research as collaborators.
result: Metformin 1000 mg twice daily or placebo was added to insulin. The primary composite of fetal and neonatal outcomes did not differ (40% against 40%, relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.26, p = 0.86). Metformin-treated women had lower HbA1c at 34 weeks (41.0 mmol/mol, SD 8.5, against 43.2, SD 10; 5.90% against 6.10%, p = 0.015), needed less insulin (1.1 against 1.5 units per kg per day, difference -0.4, -0.5 to -0.2, p < 0.0001), gained less weight (7.2 kg against 9.0 kg, difference -1.8, -2.7 to -0.9, p < 0.0001) and had fewer caesarean births (125 of 234, 53%, against 148 of 236, 63%; relative risk 0.85, 0.73 to 0.99, p = 0.031); hypertensive disorders did not differ (23% against 23%). Metformin-exposed infants weighed less (mean birthweight 3156 g, SD 742, against 3375 g, SD 742; difference -218 g, -353 to -82, p = 0.002), fewer were above the 97th centile for birthweight (20, 9%, against 34, 15%; relative risk 0.58, 0.34 to 0.97, p = 0.041) and fewer weighed 4000 g or more (28, 12%, against 44, 19%; 0.65, 0.43 to 0.99, p = 0.046), with lower adiposity measures. Small-for-gestational-age infants numbered 30 (13%) with metformin against 15 (7%) with placebo, relative risk 1.96 (1.10 to 3.64, p = 0.026). Cord C-peptide did not differ. The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal, 38 in each group. The authors conclude that the lower adiposity and infant size measurements produced fewer large infants but a higher proportion of small-for-gestational-age infants, and that understanding the implications of these effects on infants will be important in advising patients considering metformin in pregnancy.
